newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine's new reform chief vows action on budget.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine's new reform chief vows action on budget.

text.p: Ukraine's new economic reform chief vowed on Friday to break a five-month deadlock between government and parliament over this year's budget and win back the trust of foreign investors.

"People have been saying about me: 'A young boy has come along, just 37 years old, who doesn't know the work of the government,'" said new Deputy Prime Minister Serhiy Tyhypko, former head of Privatbank, one of the top five commercial banks.
"But I can tell you one thing. I am a very good manager," added Tyhypko, whose appointment raised eyebrows among some economists concerned that he has no government experience.
"Under me the bank's budget was approved in late January for the fourth time in a row," he told reporters.
Tyhypko faces a mammoth task trying to get this year's budget and a package of tax reforms through parliament, which is dominated by conservatives resistant to reforms.

His predecessor was Viktor Pynzenyk, who won the trust of international lending bodies but resigned on Monday in anger, accusing parliament and government of lacking the political will to push through the budget and tax reforms underpinning it.
Pynzenk, an economics professor, said government officials were too worried about their own pockets to approve tax reforms which would have reined in monopolies and limited corruption.

A series of foreign companies have left Ukraine in recent months or reduced their operations, notably U.S. telecoms giant Motorola which pulled out of a potential half-a-billion dollar mobile phone deal, complaining of "ever-changing" rules.
"We have to try to renew the deal somehow...At least I will try to talk to Motorola," Tyhypko said.
But he said the main thing was to get a state structure in place devoted to dealing with foreign investors -- which he said would be achieved in two to three months.
"I am ready to personally support any serious foreign investor, ready to personally support his interests," he added.

Tyhypko said it was clear that badly-paid government officials would demand payments since working with foreign investors was not even their job. "When this structure is created corruption will be reduced. That is clear," he said.
Tyhypko also sought to reassure international donors like the International Monetary Fund, which has already lent $867 million in a stand-by loan which expired in February.
"Ukraine has never been in such a tough position... Foreign donors gave us advances in the hope we would somehow speed up reforms but we have done the opposite," he said.
"I will do everything I can and employ all my strengths to move this process forward," he added.
Diplomats said this week that reforms had stalled so badly that Ukraine was closer than ever to losing its status as the third biggest recipient of U.S. aid.
Washington, with a keen interest in prolonging Ukraine's five years of independence from Moscow, has led the charge to give money to Ukraine, diplomats say.
Tyhypko said he was undertaking "very serious preparation" for his first meeting with the IMF and joked: "I am horror-struck about this meeting".
